items.prompt: Fig. VIS-6116-3.7-01 is a photomicrograph of a transverse section of a young dicotyledonous root. Identify the star-shaped tissue at the centre and the tissue lying between the arms of the star.

items.prompt: Explain water entry into a root hair when soil water has a higher water potential than the cell contents.
items.canonical_answer: Water enters by osmosis. It moves across the partially permeable cell membrane, down the water potential gradient from the soil water into the cell, so the cell gains water.
marking_guidance: 1 mark: names the process as osmosis.
1 mark: states that water then moves across the partially permeable cell membrane, down the water potential gradient, so the cell gains water.

items.prompt: Explain the complete route and mechanism of water movement from moist soil through a plant to the air. Assume soil water has a higher water potential than root hair contents.
items.canonical_answer: Water enters root hairs by osmosis. It crosses the cortex, through cell walls and cells, into the xylem. Water evaporates from the moist surfaces of mesophyll cells, and this pulls a continuous column of water up the xylem. Water vapour diffuses out through the stomata into the air.
marking_guidance: 1 mark: water enters the root hairs by osmosis.
1 mark: it then crosses the cortex, through cell walls and cells, into the xylem.
1 mark: evaporation from the surfaces of mesophyll cells pulls a continuous column of water up the xylem.
1 mark: water vapour diffuses out through the stomata, so water is lost to the air.

items.prompt: Explain why a shoot supplied with water still wilts after a narrow section of its xylem is crushed, although its phloem remains intact.
items.canonical_answer: Crushed xylem restricts water flow to the leaves. Transpiration then exceeds replacement, so leaf cells lose turgor.
marking_guidance: 1 mark: the crushed xylem cannot carry water up to the leaves (phloem does not transport water).

items.prompt: A learner says that one transport tissue carries water up from the roots to the leaves and also carries sucrose from the leaves to a growing bud. Explain the error and name the tissue that carries each substance.
items.canonical_answer: Two different tissues are involved. Xylem carries water and mineral ions up from the roots. Phloem carries sucrose and amino acids from the leaves to the bud and other regions of use or storage.

items.prompt: Describe an investigation using a suitable stain to find the water pathway in a leafy shoot.
items.canonical_answer: Change the supplied liquid: teacher-selected dilute stain or plain water. Measure the location and height of internal colour after a fixed time. Use similar shoots, liquid volumes and environments. Cut shoots under water, stand them in the liquids and examine safe teacher-cut stem sections and leaf veins. Repeat with several shoots in each treatment.

1 mark: the dependent variable is measured: which tissues are coloured, and how high the colour has reached, after a fixed time.
1 mark: at least two variables are kept the same, such as similar shoots, volume of liquid, time and temperature.
1 mark: the stems are cut under water before being stood in the liquids, so air does not block the xylem.

items.prompt: Define transpiration.
items.canonical_answer: Loss of water vapour from plant leaves by evaporation of water at the surfaces of mesophyll cells followed by diffusion of water vapour through the stomata.

1 mark: the water vapour then diffuses out of the leaf through the stomata. The definition must include both processes and refer to loss of water vapour from the leaves.

marking_guidance: 1 mark: gives the reason that damaged cilia move mucus out less effectively.
1 mark: so mucus and trapped pathogens stay in the airways, because they are not swept out, which leads to more infections.
items.provenance: Original Codex authoring for Biology 6116; marking guidance proposed, not official.

items.prompt: A learner says that tar is the part of tobacco smoke that both reduces the oxygen the blood can carry and stops the cilia clearing mucus from the airways. Explain the mistake and name the smoke component responsible for each effect.
items.canonical_answer: Tar does damage the cilia, so mucus is not cleared from the airways. It is carbon monoxide, not tar, that combines with haemoglobin and reduces the oxygen the blood carries.
marking_guidance: 1 mark: explains the mistake, that carbon monoxide instead of tar combines with haemoglobin and reduces the oxygen the blood carries.
1 mark: names tar as the component that damages the cilia, so mucus is not cleared.
items.provenance: Original Codex authoring for Biology 6116; marking guidance proposed, not official.

items.prompt: State the chronic obstructive respiratory disease that tobacco smoking can cause.
items.canonical_answer: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD).
marking_guidance: 1 mark: names the disease, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD).
